 REDDING, Calif. — Shasta County voters are being asked to weigh in on two familiar ballot measures that would amend the county charter, after similar proposals failed in 2024.
 Measure E would restrict the county’s use of eminent domain to transfer private property to another private owner. The proposal previously appeared on the 2024 ballot as Measure P and lost by 358 votes.
 Supporters say the earlier measure failed because voters did not fully understand it. Under Measure E, the county would be prevented from taking private property without the owner’s consent if the county plans to transfer it to another private party.
 Measure E on the Shasta County Ballot. Nov. 2 (KRCR) 
 California law allows the government to appropriate land from private parties, even if those parties do not want to sell, as long as that land is put towards public use. The government is also able to use eminent domain to acquire property for private entities in this way, only if those entities are also putting the land toward public use . Under Proposition 99 , some limits on these transfers do exist, prohibiting the government from using eminent domain to take a single-family home for the purpose of transferring it to another private party. Some exceptions do apply.
 Under Measure E, the restriction would be extended to all private property. Supporters argue the change would better protect property owners, while opponents say an added county restriction is unnecessary.
 County records show Shasta County has not used eminent domain to transfer property to a private owner in the last 50 years. Measure F would change how Shasta County fills vacancies in certain elected offices, including sheriff and district attorney. A similar proposal, Measure Q , was rejected in 2024, with more than 58% voting "no."
 Under Measure F, if an office becomes vacant and a regularly scheduled election is within 12 months of the vacancy, voters will choose the replacement at that election. If no election is scheduled within that time frame, the Shasta County Board of Supervisors would appoint someone, but only with at least four of the five supervisors approving. Currently, the board can appoint a replacement with a simple majority of three votes.
 Measure F on the Shasta County Ballot. Nov. 2 (KRCR) 
 Supporters say the change would give voters a chance to select a replacement. Opponents say it could leave an office without a permanent elected leader for up to a year.
 Measures E and F are separate questions on the Shasta County ballot. A yes vote would approve the proposed charter changes, while a no vote would keep the current rules in place.
